teaser: A skill behaviour policy compares what a skill says, what it can do and what it is given, then generates the control; measured on 899 skills.
core_idea: The claim that one in twenty Claude skills is built to hack you overstates a study that found 5.2% of marketplace skills with patterns suggesting malicious intent; a skill behaviour policy instead compares the described mandate, the actual mandate found as features in a skill's files, and the grant of the environment it runs in, records dual-use features with their reasons rather than verdicts, and generates hooks and sandbox settings that bring the grant down to the description; on 899 public skills, 812 reach beyond their own scripts, 782 through one third-party tool server, 39 have undescribed features, and an honest skill with the whole lethal trifecta still needs a control that a malice scanner would not ask for.

figures.caption: A skill behaviour policy: three mandates, two gaps, one control. What the description says, what the skill's files and instructions can do, and what the environment grants. Actual minus described is the suspicious part; grant minus actual is the reach nobody asked for; the control brings the grant down to the described mandate.

899 skills from three public sources, every file read as text and nothing run: what they can reach, and what their descriptions leave out. 812 can reach something beyond their own scripts, 782 of them through one third-party tool server; 39 have a feature their description does not mention; none was obfuscated, and none sets allowed-tools.

One skill, end to end: developer-growth-analysis. An honest description and the whole lethal trifecta: it reads your Claude Code chat history, searches HackerNews, and sends a report to Slack through a third-party tool server. The policy states the minimal grant and the reach on Claude Code, and generates a hook, tested on nine fixed inputs, with what it cannot see and what stays an expectation.
